lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! Today, your own provisioning builds the Slurm cluster, and sind just brings the nodes.
Your Slurm comes from Ansible roles or Chef cookbooks. But when did they last build a cluster from scratch?
Say you maintain the Slurm roles for your site. You want to run them end to end, on fresh nodes, as often as you like.
All you need is sind, Docker, and the provisioning code you already have.
First, a quick refresher. The first process in a container gets PID one. Usually, that's the one program the container exists for.
When that program exits, the container stops. Nothing else runs inside: no service manager, no SSH daemon.
sind nodes run systemd as PID one instead. It starts services like munge and sshd in dependency order, and supervises them.
When the container stops, systemd shuts everything down cleanly. So to your provisioning, a node looks like a real machine.
Normally, sind does it all: containers, networks, DNS and SSH access, a shared munge key, and Slurm on top.
An unmanaged cluster keeps all of that, munge included, but stops short of Slurm.
But the Slurm configuration directory stays empty, and slurmctld and slurmd are not started. That part is yours.
In the config, the controller gets managed false. That single flag covers the whole cluster: every node is unmanaged.
Slurm sections in this file are rejected, because sind writes no Slurm configuration.
Create the cluster as usual. This time, sind is done once systemd, sshd and munge run on each node.
The stock node image has Slurm installed, but not enabled.
Now, provision Slurm. By hand, it starts with a slurm.conf, written to the controller over sind ssh.
The Slurm configuration is one volume for all nodes, like an NFS share. It's writable on the controllers, and read-only everywhere else.
The controller also needs a small cgroup config, and then its slurmctld can start.
Each worker then gets its slurmd, and srun sends a first job across both of them.
Ansible and Chef do the same as root, over SSH. Pull in the SSH config from sind, and address each node by its name.
So your inventory lists the controller, the submitter and both workers, by their full names.
A few things to keep in mind. Write Slurm files on a controller, because every node reads the same files.
The munge key belongs to sind. Its directory is read-only, so your recipes must leave it alone.
And sind get cluster reports only munge and sshd. Check Slurm itself with sinfo, and with the slurmctld logs.
Now, your own node image. It needs systemd as init, and a shell, because sind starts every node through a short shell script.
sshd and munge must be enabled, but leave out the SSH host keys. Each node generates its own on first boot.
On an unmanaged cluster, the image may even leave Slurm out, for your provisioning to install.
In the Dockerfile, set the stop signal that systemd takes as a shutdown request, and declare the shared volumes.
So: managed false hands Slurm to your tooling, your recipes reach every node over SSH, and your image needs systemd, sshd and munge.
Your roles, tested on fresh nodes! Next up: let your assistant drive. See you there!
